''' Joseph Frederick Engelberger''' (July 26, 1925 – December 1, 2015) was an American physicist,  engineer and entrepreneur. Often regarded as the "Father of Robotics". Licensing the original patent awarded to inventor [[George Devol]], Engelberger developed the first [[industrial robot]] in the United States, the [[Unimate]], in the 1950s. Later, he worked as an entrepreneur and vocal advocate of robotic technology beyond the manufacturing plant in a variety of fields, including service industries, health care, and space exploration.

==Biography==

===Early life and education===
Joseph Frederick Engelberger was born on July 26, 1925, in [[Brooklyn]], New York.<ref>{{Cite news |url=https://www.washingtonpost.com/national/health-science/joseph-f-engelberger-pioneer-of-robotics-dies-at-90/2015/12/04/02f21612-99d0-11e5-b499-76cbec161973_story.html |title=Joseph F. Engelberger, pioneer of robotics, dies at 90 |newspaper=[[The Washington Post]] |date=2015-12-04 |issn=0190-8286 |language=en-US |first=Emily |last=Langer}}</ref> He grew up in [[Connecticut]] during the [[Great Depression]], but later returned to New York City for his college education.<ref name="angelo">''Robotics: A Reference Guide to the New Technology'' (2006) by Joseph A. Angelo {{ISBN|978-1573563376}}, pp. 104–5</ref>

Engelberger received his [[Bachelor of Science|B.S.]] in physics in 1946, and [[Master of Science|M.S.]] in Electrical Engineering in 1949 from Columbia University.<ref>''Robotics, Vision and Control: Fundamental Algorithms in MATLAB'' (2011) by Peter Corke {{ISBN|978-3642201431}}, pp. 3</ref> He worked as an engineer with [[Manning, Maxwell and Moore]], where he met inventor [[George Devol]] at a [[Westport, Connecticut|Westport]] cocktail party in 1956,<ref name="bloomberg">{{cite news|url=https://www.bloomberg.com/bw/stories/1997-03-02/invasion-of-the-robots|work=Businessweek|title=Invasion Of The Robots|date=March 2, 1997|access-date=December 1, 2015}}</ref> two years after Devol had designed and patented a rudimentary industrial robotic arm.<ref name="angelo"/><ref name="botmag">{{cite news|url=http://www.botmag.com/the-rise-and-fall-of-unimation-inc-story-of-robotics-innovation-triumph-that-changed-the-world/|title=THE RISE AND FALL OF UNIMATION, INC. – Story of robotics innovation & triumph that changed the world!|date=December 2, 2010|first=George|last=Munson|access-date=December 1, 2015|archive-date=December 8, 2015|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20151208123700/http://www.botmag.com/the-rise-and-fall-of-unimation-inc-story-of-robotics-innovation-triumph-that-changed-the-world/|url-status=dead}}</ref><ref name="henderson">''Modern Robotics: Building Versatile Machines'' (2006) by Harry Henderson {{ISBN|978-0816057450}}, pp. 31–4</ref> However, Manning, Maxwell and Moore was sold and Engelberger's division was closed that year.<ref name="leider">''Robots: Explore the World of Robots and How They Work for Us'' (2015) by Rick Leider {{ISBN|978-1632204394}}</ref>

===Unimation===
Finding himself jobless but with a business partner and an idea, Engelberger co-founded [[Unimation]] with Devol, creating the world's first robotics company.<ref name="botmag"/><ref name="leider"/> In 1957, he also founded Consolidated Controls Corporation.<ref name="henderson"/> As president of Unimation, Engelberger collaborated with Devol to engineer and produce an industrial robot under the brand name [[Unimate]]. The first Unimate robotic arm was installed at a [[General Motors]] Plant in [[Ewing Township, New Jersey]], in 1961.<ref name="razor">{{cite web|url=https://www.razorrobotics.com/robotics/Unimate|title=Unimate|publisher=Razor Robotics|access-date=December 1, 2015|url-status=dead|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20151208044551/https://www.razorrobotics.com/robotics/Unimate|archive-date=December 8, 2015}}</ref><ref name="nytimes">{{cite news|url=https://www.nytimes.com/2011/08/16/business/george-devol-developer-of-robot-arm-dies-at-99.html?_r=0|title=George C. Devol, Inventor of Robot Arm, Dies at 99|date=August 15, 2011|access-date=December 1, 2015|first=Jeremy|last=Pearce|work=The New York Times }}</ref>

The introduction of robotics to the manufacturing process effectively transformed the automotive industry,<ref name="botmag"/><ref name="move">{{cite news|url=http://electronicdesign.com/embedded/joseph-engelberger-robotics-move-industry-space-elder-care|title=Joseph Engelberger: Robotics Move From Industry To Space To Elder Care|first=Doris|last=Kilbane|date=December 1, 2008|access-date=December 1, 2015|work=Electronic Design}}</ref><ref name="robotics">{{cite news|url=http://www.robotics.org/content-detail.cfm/Industrial-Robotics-News/Joseph-F-Engelberger-Father-of-Robotics/content_id/5840|title=Joseph F. Engelberger, Father of Robotics|date=December 1, 2015|access-date=December 1, 2015|agency=Robotics Industries Association}}</ref> with [[Chrysler]] and the [[Ford Motor Company]] soon following General Motors' lead and installing Unimates in their manufacturing facilities.<ref name="nytimes"/> The rapid adoption of the technology also provided Unimation with a working business model: after selling the first Unimate at a $35,000 loss, as demand increased, the company was able to begin building the robotic arms for significantly less and thus began to turn a substantial profit.<ref name="spice">{{cite news|url=https://www.post-gazette.com/news/science/2003/11/11/4-robots-clank-into-Hall-of-Fame-2-fictional-2-real/stories/200311110096|title=4 robots clank into Hall of Fame; 2 fictional, 2 real|work=Pittsburgh Post-Gazette|date=November 11, 2003|access-date=December 1, 2015|first=Byron|last=Spice}}</ref> Over the next two decades, the Japanese took the lead by investing heavily in robots to replace people performing certain tasks. In Japan, Engelberger was widely hailed as a key player in the postwar ascendancy of Japanese manufacturing quality and efficiency.<ref name="angelo"/>

In 1966, Engelberger and a Unimate robot appeared on ''[[The Tonight Show Starring Johnny Carson]]''. In the segment, the robot poured a beer, sank a golf putt, and directed the band.<ref name="angelo"/>

An early proponent of increased investment in robotic systems, Engelberger published articles and gave congressional testimony on the value of using automation in space long before the successes of [[NASA]]'s [[Exploration of Mars#NASA|Mars landers]], ''[[Galileo (spacecraft)|Galileo]]'', and other unmanned space science missions. He also consulted for NASA on the use of robotics in space exploration.<ref name="move"/><ref name="robotics"/>

Unimation purchased [[Victor Scheinman]]'s Vicarm Inc. in 1977, and with Scheinman's help, the company created and began producing the [[Programmable Universal Machine for Assembly]] (PUMA), an all-electric robotic arm, designed to facilitate an [[arm solution]] that allowed full computer control using Scheinman's cutting-edge VAL programming language. The automotive companies that had been Unimation's earliest and most reliable clients began moving away from the use of hydraulically powered robotic arms, like the Unimate, in the early 1980s in favor of electric motors, a change that Engelberger vehemently opposed. Sales fell, and the company was acquired by [[Westinghouse Electric Corporation|Westinghouse]] in 1982 for [[United States dollar|$]]107 million.<ref name="botmag"/><ref name="keay">{{cite news|url=http://robohub.org/industrial-robotics-pioneer-joe-engelberger-turns-90/|agency=Robohub|title=Industrial robotics pioneer Joe Engelberger turns 90|last=Keay|first=Andra|date=July 26, 2015|access-date=December 1, 2015}}</ref> Engelberger, who had served as Unimation's chief executive since its inception, left the company not long thereafter.<ref name="henderson"/>

===Magnetic propulsion===
In 1963 Engelberger filed with the US Patent Office his Application Ser. No. 324,928, then a second one with Ser. No. 638,666 in 1967, and US Patent No. 3,504,868 “Space Propulsion System” was registered in 1970. Numerical pioneering propositions and ideas of Engelberger in this work may be considered as a prospective competitor with rocketry and a possible means for interstellar flight.

===HelpMate===
[[File:1993 Helpmate robots.jpg|thumb|Four Helpmate robots on the floor of Transitions Research Corporation in [[Danbury, Connecticut|Danbury]], 1993]]
After observing the help for his aging parents, Engelberger saw the robotics automations could be used in the medical field.<ref>{{cite web|url=http://electronicdesign.com/embedded/joseph-engelberger-robotics-move-industry-space-elder-care |title=StackPath |publisher=Electronicdesign.com |date= |accessdate=2023-08-21}}</ref> In 1984, Engelberger founded Transitions Research Corporation. He introduced the HelpMate, a [[mobile robot]] hospital courier, as the flagship product of his new company. He hoped to kick-start a new industry for in-home robots, but he started in 1988 by selling his first HelpMate to [[Danbury Hospital]], located in [[Danbury, Connecticut|the same Connecticut city]] where his company was based. The medical robot was successful enough that the hospital ended up purchasing another, and within a decade, well over 100 hospitals worldwide operated HelpMates, whether purchased outright or rented from Engelberger's company, which he renamed HelpMate Robotics Inc.<ref name="bloomberg"/><ref>{{cite web|url=https://spinoff.nasa.gov/spinoff2003/hm_4.html|title=A Robot to Help Make the Rounds|date=2003|access-date=December 1, 2015|publisher=NASA}}</ref>

After Engelberger was awarded the [[Japan Prize]] in 1997, Senator [[Joseph Lieberman]] of Connecticut delivered a floor speech in the [[United States Senate|U.S. Senate]] in praise and recognition of the inventor, calling HelpMate Robotics "an example of the way that a patient federal investment in science and technology can lead to new products that employ Americans and make for a better quality of life."<ref>{{cite news|url=http://capitolwords.org/date/1997/05/23/S5144-3_joseph-engelberger-and-helpmate-robotics-inc/|title=Joseph Engelberger And Helpmate Robotics, Inc.|date=May 23, 1997|access-date=December 1, 2015|agency=Capitolwords, a project of the Sunlight Foundation|url-status=dead|archive-url=https://archive.today/20151220053201/http://capitolwords.org/date/1997/05/23/S5144-3_joseph-engelberger-and-helpmate-robotics-inc/|archive-date=December 20, 2015}}</ref>

HelpMate was acquired by [[Cardinal Health]] in the late 1990s, a move Engelberger came to regret, complaining that the new owners moved away from his preferred model of renting out robots toward selling off used, depreciated models.<ref name="move"/><ref name="nocks">''The Robot: The Life Story of a Technology'' (2008) by Lisa Nocks {{ISBN|978-0801890710}}, pp. 107</ref>

===Later life===
The 2000 World Automation Congress was dedicated to Engelberger, who delivered the [[keynote]] address.<ref name="henderson"/> Even after his departure from HelpMate and well into his 80s, he remained active in the promotion and development of robots for use in [[elder care]].<ref name="keay"/> He notably discouraged the notion of [[legged robot]]s, arguing that robots should use wheels for locomotion,<ref name="spice"/> although he supported the use of robotic arms to allow the machines to interact with their surroundings.<ref name="move"/><ref name="robotics"/> He worked on developing a two-armed robot to act as a "servant-companion" to seniors with limited mobility.<ref name="angelo"/>

Engelberger died on December 1, 2015, in [[Newtown, Connecticut]],<ref name="robotics"/> a little more than four months after celebrating his 90th birthday.<ref name="mmh">{{cite news |date=July 27, 2015 |title=Joseph F. Engelberger, the "Father of Robotics," turns 90 |work=Modern Materials Handling |url=http://www.mmh.com/article/joseph_f._engelberger_the_father_of_robotics_turns_90 |access-date=December 1, 2015}}</ref>

==Publications==
Engelberger published ''Robotics in Practice'' in 1980. The book became a classic in the field and has been translated into six languages. ''Robotics in Practice'' was followed by ''Robotics in Service'' in 1989.<ref name="robotics"/><ref>''Robotics in Service'' (1989) by Joseph F. Engelberger {{ISBN|978-0262525664}}</ref> 
Engelberger received US Patent No. 3,504,868 in 1970 that gave the priority in the technology of the space magnetic propulsion to the United States of America.

==Awards and honors==
Engelberger was elected to the [[National Academy of Engineering]] in 1984. He was also honored among "The 1000 makers of the 20st Century" by ''[[The Sunday Times]]'' in 1992.<ref name="nocks"/> Additional honors include the Progress Award of the [[Society of Manufacturing Engineers]],<ref name="henderson"/> the 1982 Nyselius Award from the American Die Casting Institution, the 1982 [[ASME Leonardo Da Vinci Award|Leonardo da Vinci Award]] of the [[American Society of Mechanical Engineers]], the 1982 American Machinist Award, the 1983 Golden Omega Award at the Electrical Electronics Insulation Conference,<ref name="robotics1">{{cite web |title=JOSEPH ENGELBERGER // The Father of Robotics |url=http://www.robotics.org/joseph-engelberger/about.cfm |access-date=December 1, 2015 |publisher=Robotics Industries Association}}</ref> the 1983 McKechnie Award from the [[University of Liverpool]],<ref>{{cite news|url=http://www.siliconinvestor.com/readmsg.aspx?msgid=5867485|title=Financial Intranet, Inc. Today Announced the Appointment of Joseph F. Engelberger to Its Board of Directors|agency=Business Wire|date=September 29, 1998|access-date=December 1, 2015}}</ref> the 1984 Egleston Medal from [[Columbia University]],<ref>{{cite web|url=http://cuengineeringalumni.org/ceaa-awards/egleston-medal/|publisher=Columbia Engineering Alumni Association|title=The Thomas Egleston Medal for Distinguished Engineering Achievement|access-date=December 1, 2015|url-status=dead|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20151208151818/http://cuengineeringalumni.org/ceaa-awards/egleston-medal/|archive-date=December 8, 2015}}</ref> the 1997 Beckman Award for pioneering and original research in the field of automation,<ref name="robotics"/> and the 1997 [[Japan Prize]], the highest Japanese technology honor, for the establishment of the robot industry.<ref>{{cite web|url=http://www.japanprize.jp/en/prize_prof_1997_engel.html|title=Laureates of the Japan Prize|publisher=The Japan Prize Foundation|access-date=December 1, 2015}}</ref> He also received the [[IEEE Robotics and Automation Award]] in 2004.<ref name="henderson"/>

==Legacy==
The [[Robotics Industries Association]] (now the A3 - [[Association for Advancing Automation]]) annually presents the Joseph F. Engelberger Awards to "persons who have contributed outstandingly to the furtherance of the science and practice of robotics." The award was first given in 1977.<ref name="henderson"/>

Engelberger's most famous co-invention, the [[Unimate]] industrial robotic arm, was among the first inductees into the [[Robot Hall of Fame]] in 2003.<ref name="razor"/><ref name="spice"/>
